title: Word Professional Documents
description: Create reports, proposals, and templates that look intentional. Use styles, sections, tables, references, and review tools like a professional.

badge.name: Document Architect
badge.description: Awarded for completing Word Professional Documents and its final assessment.

outcomes: Structure long documents with headings and styles
Control page size, margins, sections, headers, and footers
Build clean tables and captions that stay together
Create a navigation pane and automatic table of contents
Collaborate with comments and tracked changes
Produce a polished proposal from a reusable template
prerequisites: Microsoft Word 2016 or newer, or Microsoft 365
A document you can edit or a blank file
No prior Word formatting experience required
tools: Optional: a PDF reader for checking the exported document

modules.title: Foundations
modules.summary: The workspace, the views, and the habits that keep files safe.

content.text: Word looks simple because the page is in the middle. The power lives in the tools around it: the ribbon, the navigation pane, the status bar, and the styles gallery.

The ribbon groups commands by task: Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Review, and View. The Home tab is where you format text, the Insert tab adds objects, and References creates tables of contents and citations. Do not hunt through every tab; learn where the common groups live.

content.title: Turn on the Navigation pane early
content.text: View > Navigation Pane shows headings when you use built-in heading styles. It is the fastest way to move around a long document and to spot missing structure.

content.question: Which feature helps you move between headings in a long document?
content.explanation: The Navigation pane lists heading styles and lets you jump between sections.

lessons.title: Text, paragraphs, and the invisible layer

content.text: Most formatting problems in Word begin with invisible characters. Turning on formatting marks shows where paragraphs, spaces, tabs, and section breaks actually are.

Press `Ctrl + *` or click the paragraph mark on the Home tab to show formatting marks. A pilcrow (¶) ends a paragraph. A small arrow is a tab, a dot is a space, and a dotted line may mark a page or section break.

items: Press Enter to start a new paragraph; do not use empty paragraphs to create page breaks.
Use `Ctrl + Enter` for a deliberate page break.
Use paragraph spacing rather than multiple blank lines between paragraphs.
Use tabs or table columns, not a string of spaces, to align text.
Use `Ctrl + Shift + 8` to toggle formatting marks when troubleshooting.

content.title: Empty paragraphs are a trap
content.text: They look harmless until content moves. A heading then pushes the next page, and your carefully spaced document falls apart. Use paragraph spacing and section breaks instead.

content.question: What is the cleanest way to create space between paragraphs?
options: Use paragraph spacing before or after
Add spaces at the end of the line
content.explanation: Paragraph spacing is part of the paragraph style and survives edits and reflowing.

content.text: A professional document is not just well formatted. It is saved in the right format, named clearly, and recoverable if something goes wrong.
Save editable work as `.docx`. Export a finished copy as PDF when the layout must be fixed for sharing or printing. Keep the source file so the document can still be edited later.

items.title: Name the file for humans
items.text: Use a name that includes the document type, client or project, and date: `Proposal_Northwind_2026-11.docx`.

items.title: Save to a known location
items.text: Use OneDrive, SharePoint, or a clear folder structure. Do not rely on Downloads.

items.title: Turn on AutoSave when available
items.text: Microsoft 365 can save continuously to OneDrive. If it is unavailable, use Ctrl + S often.

items.title: Export a PDF for sharing
items.text: File > Export > Create PDF/XPS. Check the exported file, especially page breaks and embedded fonts.

items.title: Keep the editable source
items.text: The PDF is a snapshot. The `.docx` is the working document.

content.title: Version before big changes
content.text: Save a copy with 'v2' or a date before a major rewrite. It is faster than trying to undo a chain of edits later.

content.question: Which format is best for sharing a finished document whose layout must not change?
content.explanation: PDF preserves the intended layout across devices, while .docx remains the editable source.

modules.title: Styles and structure
modules.summary: Let Word do the formatting work, consistently.

content.text: A style is a named bundle of formatting. Apply Heading 1 to a chapter title once and every chapter title can look the same.

Do not format each heading manually with a bigger font and bold. Use the built-in Heading 1, Heading 2, and Normal styles. The Navigation pane, automatic table of contents, and accessibility tools all understand those styles.

rows: Keeps line spacing and font consistent

items.title: Apply the built-in style
items.text: Place the cursor in the heading and click Heading 1, or use Ctrl + Alt + 1.

items.title: Modify once
items.text: Right-click the style in the gallery and choose Modify to change its font, colour, and spacing.

items.title: Update to match
items.text: After changing a style, all text using that style updates.

items.title: Keep styles clean
items.text: Avoid manual bold and size changes on top of a heading. They hide the structure.

content.title: Direct formatting wins over styles
content.text: If you use the Bold button on a heading, that direct formatting stays even if you change the heading style. Use the style itself to make the change everywhere.

content.question: Why use Heading 1 instead of manually making text large and bold?
options: It creates real document structure used by navigation and the TOC
content.explanation: Built-in headings carry semantic structure, not just appearance.

content.text: A long document is a map. Headings are the landmarks; the Navigation pane is the map viewer.

Use Heading 1 for major sections, Heading 2 for subsections, and Heading 3 only when the content genuinely needs another level. A clear outline is easier to write, easier to review, and easier for readers to scan.

items: Aim for a logical outline before perfecting formatting.
Do not skip levels just because a heading looks the right size; change the style if needed.
Use the Navigation pane to drag sections into a better order.
Keep heading text short and descriptive.
Use the outline view for structural work without visual distractions.

content.title: Write the outline first
content.text: Create the headings and a sentence under each one before writing paragraphs. It reveals gaps in the argument while changes are still cheap.

content.question: What does the Navigation pane use to show a document outline?
content.explanation: Headings applied with built-in styles appear in the Navigation pane.

content.text: An automatic table of contents is a field, not a list typed by hand. It updates as headings move, which is exactly when a manual TOC becomes wrong.

Place the cursor where the contents should go, then choose References > Table of Contents and pick a style. Word builds the entries from heading styles. If a heading is missing, check that it uses Heading 1-3.

items.title: Apply heading styles
items.text: Every section and subsection should use a heading style.

items.title: Insert the TOC
items.text: References > Table of Contents > Automatic Table.

items.title: Update after edits
items.text: Click the TOC and choose Update Table, or press F9.

items.title: Update page numbers only or the whole table
items.text: Choose the whole table when headings changed; page numbers only when just pagination moved.

items.title: Check the entries
items.text: Ensure no stray heading appears and the page numbers match the printed document.

content.title: The TOC is only as good as the headings
content.text: If you styled headings manually, the TOC cannot see them. Fix the structure first, then regenerate the field.

content.question: What should you do after adding or renaming a section?
content.explanation: An automatic TOC must be updated to reflect current headings and page numbers.

modules.title: Layout, sections, and tables
modules.summary: Control pages, headers, and the objects that carry information.

content.text: A section break is a dividing line in document behaviour. It lets one part of a document have different margins, orientation, headers, or page numbering from another.

A page break simply moves content to the next page. A section break starts a new section, which can have its own layout. Use section breaks for a landscape appendix, a cover page with no header, or a new chapter that restarts page numbering.

rows: Starting a new page in a report

items.title: Open the header
items.text: Insert > Header or double-click the top margin.

items.title: Unlink from previous
items.text: For a section with a different header, turn off Link to Previous before editing.

items.title: Add fields
items.text: Insert page number, document title, or date through the Header & Footer tools.

items.title: Check each section
items.text: Scroll through the document and confirm the header, footer, and numbering behave as intended.

content.title: Headers can change without warning
content.text: If a header unexpectedly disappears, check whether the section is linked to the previous one. Unlink it before making changes.

content.question: Which break allows a single document to have a landscape page in the middle?
content.explanation: A new section can have its own orientation, margins, and page setup.

content.text: A Word table is a layout tool, not a spreadsheet. It is excellent for aligned information, but formulas and large datasets belong in Excel.

Insert a table with a defined number of columns, not with spaces or tabs. Use table styles for consistent shading and borders, then adjust only what you need. Set the header row to repeat across pages, and prevent rows from splitting awkwardly across a page break.

items: Use a header row and repeat it on every page.
Keep columns wide enough for the longest realistic value.
Avoid merging cells inside a data table.
Use Table Properties > Row > Allow row to break across pages only when needed.
Add a caption above or below the table and reference it in the text.
Do not use a table as a page layout hack; use columns and margins.

content.title: Repeat header rows
content.text: Select the header row, open Table Properties > Row, and tick Repeat as header row at the top of each page. This is essential for long tables.

content.question: Where should large numerical datasets normally live?
options: In Excel, with a summary in Word
content.explanation: Excel is designed for calculations and large data. Word is better for presenting the result.

content.text: Images should support the argument and stay attached to their captions. The difference between a polished report and a frustrating one is often object placement.

Use In Line with Text for images that should flow with the document. Use a fixed position only when a floating layout is essential, and check it on every page. Add a caption with References > Insert Caption so figures can be numbered and cross-referenced.

rows: Reports, proposals, documents that will be edited

content.title: Floating images can wander
content.text: If a floating image jumps to another page after edits, right-click it, check the layout options, and consider anchoring it to a paragraph or converting it to in-line.

content.question: Which image placement is usually safest in a document that will be edited?
content.explanation: In-line images move predictably with the surrounding text.

modules.title: Review, refine, collaborate
modules.summary: Make documents accurate, accessible, and easy to review together.

content.text: Track Changes turns editing into a visible conversation. It is essential when someone else needs to see what changed and why.

Turn it on in Review > Track Changes. Insertions and deletions are attributed to you. Comments can discuss a choice without changing the text. Use both tools for their intended purpose: tracked changes for edits, comments for questions and context.

items.title: Turn on Track Changes
items.text: Review > Track Changes. Confirm the status indicator is active.

items.title: Edit normally
items.text: Every insertion and deletion appears as a revision.

items.title: Comment on decisions
items.text: Select the relevant text and choose New Comment. Ask a clear question.

items.title: Review with context
items.text: Use Reviewing Pane or the markup view to see all changes.

items.title: Accept or reject deliberately
items.text: Accept All is not a review. Read each change that matters.

items.title: Turn it off before final formatting
items.text: Otherwise your final clean-up edits become new tracked changes.

content.title: Tracked changes can hide in a PDF
content.text: Before sharing, decide whether to show markup or accept it. Review > Display for Review controls what the reader sees, and File > Inspect Document can find leftover metadata.

content.question: When should Track Changes typically be turned off?
content.explanation: Turning it off for final clean-up prevents every formatting adjustment from becoming a tracked revision.

content.text: Find and Replace is a precision tool. Used carefully, it can fix repeated errors in seconds. Used carelessly, it can change every 'form' to 'from' in a legal document.

Use `Ctrl + H`, search for a distinctive phrase, and choose Replace or Find Next. For repeated formatting changes, use Replace Format. For pattern-based work, explore wildcards, but preview the matches first.

items: Search for whole words to avoid changing substrings.
Use Find All to see how many matches exist before replacing.
Use Replace Format to update a font or paragraph setting consistently.
Check headers, footers, text boxes, and footnotes separately.
Run Editor or the spell checker after structural changes.

content.title: The two-pass proof
content.text: First pass for structure and meaning; second pass for spelling, spacing, and consistency. Reading backwards can help you notice typos that your brain auto-corrects.

content.question: What is the safest first step before Replace All?
options: Use Find All to preview the matches
content.explanation: Previewing matches prevents unintended global changes.

content.text: A document that nobody can navigate is not finished. Accessibility checks catch structural problems before they reach the reader.

Use real headings, alt text for meaningful images, readable table headers, and descriptive link text. A link called 'Click here' tells a screen-reader user nothing; 'Download the 2026 safety policy' does.

items: Use built-in heading styles rather than visual imitation.
Add alt text to images that carry meaning; mark decorative images as decorative.
Use table header rows and avoid merged cells in data tables.
Do not rely on colour alone to convey meaning.
Use descriptive hyperlink text.
Check the document with Word's accessibility checker.
Remove leftover comments and tracked changes before final delivery.
Run Inspect Document if the file will be shared externally.

content.title: The accessibility checker is a starting point
content.text: It can catch missing alt text and heading issues, not whether the writing is clear. Read the document as a first-time reader would.

content.question: Which hyperlink text is most accessible?
content.explanation: Descriptive link text explains the destination out of context.

modules.title: Capstone: a polished proposal
modules.summary: Plan, build, review, and hand over a professional document.

content.text: A proposal is an argument with a practical outcome. Before formatting, decide who reads it, what they need to decide, and what evidence they need.

Use a simple structure: context, problem, proposed approach, scope, timeline, cost, risks, and next step. Not every proposal needs every section, but the reader should never have to search for the ask.

rows: What is this and why now?
What do I need to do?

content.title: Write the summary last, place it first
content.text: The executive summary is easier to write after the argument is complete, even though the reader sees it first.

content.question: What should an executive summary focus on?
options: The decision, rationale, and next step
content.explanation: A summary should let a busy reader understand the proposal and what happens next.

content.text: Build the proposal with styles and sections from the start. Retrofitting structure onto a manually formatted document is unnecessary work.

Create a cover page in its own section, a table of contents, body headings, a table for the timeline, and a short appendix. Use page numbers and a footer. Check that the header does not appear on the cover if you do not want it there.

items.title: Set page size and margins
items.text: Use the intended paper size and a margin that leaves room for binding if needed.

items.title: Create the cover section
items.text: Insert a Next Page section break after the cover.

items.title: Apply heading styles
items.text: Heading 1 for major sections, Heading 2 for subsections.

items.title: Insert the TOC
items.text: Place it after the cover and before the body.

items.title: Add tables and captions
items.text: Use repeat header rows for long tables and a consistent caption style.

items.title: Add page numbers and footer
items.text: Decide whether numbering restarts after the cover.

items.title: Run the checks
items.text: Update the TOC, check page breaks, proof, accessibility, and exported PDF.

content.title: Make it reusable
content.text: Once the structure is polished, save a copy as a template (.dotx). Replace the content but keep the styles and page setup. That is how a team gets consistent documents without rebuilding them.

content.question: Why build a reusable template from a good document?
options: To make every document identical in content
To preserve styles and layout while replacing content
content.explanation: A template standardises structure and design while keeping the content flexible.

content.text: The last ten percent is where a document becomes trustworthy. Check the logic, the numbers, the structure, and the reader experience.

Review in passes. First for argument and completeness. Then for structure and formatting. Then for language and consistency. Then for accessibility and export. Trying to do all four at once slows you down and misses things.

rows: Read aloud or ask a reviewer
Wrong heading levels, broken TOC, awkward page breaks
Missing alt text, vague links, table headers
Stale comments, hidden metadata, PDF layout

content.title: Print preview catches what the screen hides
content.text: Widows, orphaned headings, split tables, and blank pages are easiest to spot in the print layout.
Handover checklist

items: The title, client, and date are correct.
The table of contents is updated.
Page numbers are present and logical.
Headers and footers are correct in every section.
All comments and tracked changes are resolved or intentionally kept.
Images have meaningful alt text.
The exported PDF opens and looks correct.
The editable source is stored in the agreed location.

content.question: What is the best final check before sending a PDF?
options: Open the exported PDF and check page breaks, links, and layout
content.explanation: Exporting can reveal pagination and layout issues not visible in the editable view.

finalAssessment.title: Document Architect assessment
finalAssessment.intro: Answer all eight questions. Score 80% or higher to earn the Document Architect badge and certificate.

questions.question: Why use built-in heading styles?
options: They create structure used by navigation, the TOC, and accessibility tools
questions.explanation: Heading styles carry real document structure beyond appearance.

questions.question: Which break allows different page orientation within one document?
questions.explanation: Each section can have its own page setup, including orientation.

questions.question: What does Track Changes do?
options: Shows insertions and deletions as revisions
questions.explanation: Track Changes records edits so reviewers can accept or reject them.

questions.question: How do you make a table header repeat across pages?
options: Use Table Properties > Row > Repeat as header row
questions.explanation: The Repeat as header row option keeps the header visible on each page.

questions.question: Which image placement is usually safest in an editable report?
questions.explanation: In-line images flow predictably with surrounding content.

questions.question: Where does the detailed explanation belong in a presentation-style Word document or report?
options: In the body text and structure, not hidden in headers
questions.explanation: The body should carry the argument; headers and footers are for navigation and metadata.

questions.question: Why add alt text to an informative image?
options: To describe the image for people using screen readers
questions.explanation: Alt text makes the image's meaning available to non-visual users.

questions.question: What should you check in the exported PDF before sending it?
options: Page breaks, links, layout, and that the PDF opens correctly
questions.explanation: The PDF is the reader's experience. Verify it directly rather than assuming the export preserved everything.

questions.question: Which of the following is a best practice covered in this course?
How should you approach a new skill?
questions.explanation: Start with fundamentals and build up.

questions.question: What helps you retain what you learn?
If you get stuck on a lesson, what should you do?
options: Review earlier material and try again
questions.explanation: Reviewing and retrying is part of learning.
